title: Print the Doggone Paper!
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Stuart makes the case for a deceptively simple classroom-management tool: a printed roster on a clipboard used to track which students have received a brief moment of genuine connection (MGC). His argument centers on the word 'each' — teachers instinctively connect with outgoing students and the ones already flagged as behavior or academic concerns, but standoffish, shy, or glowering students get systematically skipped when connection is left to instinct. That gap, he argues, creates a self-perpetuating imbalance where the students who most need connection receive the least of it. His fix is mechanical rather than motivational: print a name sheet, check off each student during natural transition points in class, and don't start a new page until every name is checked. He closes by lowering the bar for execution, insisting the attempts don't need to be polished, just consistent.
points: Stuart's central insight is that the failure point in relationship-building isn't caring less — it's the word 'EACH': teachers systematically under-connect with standoffish or shy students without a tracking mechanism.

He identifies two student groups who get connection 'for free' (the outgoing and the already-flagged) and by elimination names the group being missed: quiet, glowering, or seemingly disinterested students.
The tracking system (roster + clipboard + check marks + 'don't start a new page until everyone's checked') converts a values-based intention into a mechanical, verifiable habit.
He explicitly lowers the execution bar — 'these brief attempts... DO NOT need to be perfect' — reframing the tool as sustainable low-stress practice rather than one more perfectionist obligation.
quotes: The trouble is that most teachers in the world overlook one critical word in the strategy: EACH. That word EACH is where the Credibility ground game is won or lost.
Students who are super outgoing or easy to talk to. These students don't take effort to connect with, really. They come to us. Or they are outlandishly pleasant.

These students, when we leave MGCs up to instinct, receive fewer MGCs than those two student groups I listed first. And as a result, we accidentally create a kind of a self-perpetuating imbalance in the classroom.
None of us are trying to produce this cycle. But all of us contribute to it when we don't intentionally track moments of genuine connection.
These brief attempts at genuine connection DO NOT need to be perfect (mine are often awkward). They just need to be consistent and genuine.
Just print the doggone paper and keep track of who you connect with. It'll help develop Credibility and Belonging. And sometimes, it'll even be fun.
